One stock under the microscope

A deep dive into ONE stock of the per-stock run (darts_forecast_tsmixer_marimo.py): its study, its saved best model, and new inputs. Same question as there: at the decision time, is the stock up or down at the end of the horizon, and by roughly how much?
  1. The study: every trial of the stock, and the best trial's settings
  2. Is the best trial real? Which days carry its score, and what other random seeds give
  3. Which inputs does the model use? Permutation importance and SHAP
  4. New inputs: write one as a short function, check it for look-ahead and for information, then train the best trial's settings with and without it over several seeds: does the score rise by more than the seeds move it?
Everything is scored on VALIDATION; TEST stays unread here.

Settings

The stock, the per-stock batch whose best model is studied, and the dates of that batch (the notebook checks that the saved model reproduces its score on them). SEEDS: how many random seeds every comparison trains: more seeds, smaller noise, longer runs.

1 · The study

Figure 1: every trial's end correlation on VALIDATION. The first 10 are random draws, the others chosen by the optimizer. Table 1 lists the best trials: when the top trials agree on their settings, the stock's signal is more likely real than when one trial stands out alone.

2 · How the score works

Every VALIDATION day the model makes one number at the decision: how far the stock will move by the end of the horizon, in typical moves (one ordinary minute's size, so an ordinary 60-minute stretch moves about ±8). The score, the end correlation, lines these 123 numbers up with what happened:
  • each day: (prediction − the average prediction) × (actual − the average actual), each divided by its spread; the score is the average of these products, between −1 and +1
  • a day where both sit on the same side of their averages adds (green in Figure 3), a day on opposite sides subtracts (red). A big move adds or subtracts a lot, a quiet day almost nothing. The averages, not zero: if the model's average prediction is slightly down, a smaller "down" counts as leaning up
  • only the direction and the relative size count: a model that says +0.1 before every +10 and −0.1 before every −10 scores a perfect 1. The size is set apart, by β on the held-out days
  • Figure 2: what correlations of 0, 0.1, 0.3 and 0.6 look like over 123 days. Without skill, luck alone reaches about ±0.18 in one try out of 20; the best of many tries reaches more (the bars in section 1)
  • in money (Figure 4b): a trader who buys or sells at the decision in proportion to the prediction, and closes at the horizon's end, earns per day about correlation × typical position × typical move (Grinold & Kahn's "fundamental law": return ≈ IC × volatility). In quant finance a correlation of 0.05 that holds up is already a good forecast of short-term prices; costs come off every day

4 · New inputs

How to add one: write a function of raw in the next cell and put @new_input("day" | "bar", what=..., why=...) above it. A day input returns one value per session (a static input), a bar input one value per session and minute (a past covariate, read over the model's input minutes). raw holds the stock's sessions × 390 minutes: open, high, low, close (NaN without a trade), volume, y (the minute moves in typical moves: the model's own path), market / sector (the baskets' minute moves); per session day_close (its last trade); and decision (the decision minute).
  • only what is known at the decision: a day input may use today's minutes before raw["decision"] and earlier sessions; a bar input at minute t only minutes up to t. The look-ahead check (Table 6) recomputes every input with everything after the decision hidden and flags any change
  • in typical units: values of about ±1 on an ordinary day; sl.typical(x) scales a per-minute array by the same clock minute's usual size, sl.causal_z(x) a per-session series by its own previous 60 sessions (both read earlier sessions only). Day inputs are clipped at ±4, bar inputs at ±10; NaN counts as 0
Then the two checks: Table 6 (seconds, no training) and Table 7 (training, several seeds). The seven inputs below are ideas from the literature, as a start.

Other seeds

The study trained every trial with seed 0. retrain trains the best trial's settings with 5 seeds (0 to 4): if the score was a lucky seed, the others fall back. The averaged model (the mean of the 5 seeds' predictions) is steadier than any one seed. These fits are kept: the comparisons in section 5 reuse them as their baseline.

3 · Which inputs does the model use?

Measured on the saved best model (or, with new inputs picked below, on the best trial's settings trained again with them, seed 0), in two ways that both ask what happens when an input is absent: read from another day of the stock, so it keeps its usual size and only its link to that day's outcome is cut. VALIDATION days only.
  • Permutation importance (Table 4, Figure 4; about a minute): the score again with one input scrambled, ten times each. A drop well above its sd, with most scrambles hurting: the model leans on it, and it helps on days the model never learned from. Below 0: the input hurts. Market + sector are also scrambled together (they overlap)
  • SHAP (Table 5, Figures 5 and 6; about 1.5 seconds per day): how far each input moved each prediction, signed, whether or not that helped. High here and near 0 in Table 4: the model moves with the input but gains nothing from it
  • if the model's score is within luck, every drop is small and noisy: the tables then say what this one model leans on, not what predicts

Does a new input carry information? (no training)

Table 6: every new input (and the current per-day ones, for scale) as the model sees it at the decision: a day input's value, a bar input's last minute. Its correlation with the end move on TRAIN and on VALIDATION, each with a luck z (random up/down outcomes), and with the saved model's misses (actual minus predicted end move, VALIDATION): an input that lines up with the misses carries something the model does not use yet.
  • a z beyond ±2 on TRAIN AND the same sign on VALIDATION is a candidate worth training
  • a single correlation says nothing about combinations: a weak input can still help the model through another one (Gao et al.: momentum on volatile days). Table 7 tests that
  • the model can read a bar input's whole input window, not just the last minute shown here

Does a new input make the model better? (training)

compare trains the best trial's settings (5 seeds each) as they are (the baseline: the same fits as in section 3), with each picked new input added, with all of them together, and, if ticked, with each current input dropped. Table 8 then compares every arm with the baseline on the same days and the same seeds:
  • change (paired) and its t: the seeds' mean change in end correlation; |t| > 2 is a change bigger than the seeds move it, |t| < 1 is noise
  • averaged model: the mean of the 5 seeds' predictions, scored with its luck z
  • 1st / 2nd half: the averaged model's change on each half of VALIDATION. A real gain holds in both halves; a gain from one stretch of days (like a crash) does not
  • the knobs stay the best trial's, tuned without the new input: an input the knobs do not suit can look worse than it is. Every run is appended to the stock's experiment log (Table 9), so ideas tried on earlier days stay comparable. Picking the best arm out of many is selection again: confirm a winner on TEST once, at the very end
